Throughout this page, assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]): the
analytic and cohomological suppliers invoked by the results below assume full
AC, and each item records its exact use. The definitional content below uses no
choice.

**(1) Compact Kähler manifolds.** Let $n\ge1$. A **Kähler manifold** is a complex
manifold $X$ of complex dimension $n$
([[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]) with complex structure
$J$ and a **Hermitian metric** $g$ — a Riemannian metric
([[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]) satisfying
$g(Jv,Jw)=g(v,w)$ for all tangent vectors $v,w$ — whose **real fundamental form**
$\omega(v,w)=g(Jv,w)$ is

- a smooth real 2-form, the section of $\Lambda^2T^*X$ obtained by alternating
  $g(J\cdot,\cdot)$;
- **positive**: $\omega(v,Jv)=g(Jv,Jv)>0$ for every nonzero tangent vector $v$;
- **closed**: $d\omega=0$.

The manifold is **compact Kähler** when the topological space $X$ is compact.

**Orientation.** For a complex basis $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ of a tangent space $T_xX$,
the ordered real basis $(v_1,Jv_1,\dots,v_n,Jv_n)$ is declared **positive**. This
is well defined: two complex bases differ by a complex-linear automorphism, whose
real determinant is the square of the modulus of its complex determinant and so
is positive, and the local orientations therefore glue along holomorphic charts
to a global orientation of $X$. Let $v_1,\dots,v_n$ be a $g$-orthonormal complex
frame, so $g(v_j,v_k)=\delta_{jk}$ and $g(v_j,Jv_k)=0$, and let $e_j=g(v_j,\cdot)$ and
$f_j=g(Jv_j,\cdot)$ be the metric-dual covectors. Then
$(e_1,f_1,\dots,e_n,f_n)$ is a positively oriented $g$-orthonormal coframe,
$f_j=-Je_j$ for the pullback action $(J\alpha)(v)=\alpha(Jv)$ of $J$ on
covectors, and

$$\omega=\sum_{j=1}^n e_j\wedge f_j .$$

The **oriented volume form** is the top form

$$dV:=\frac{\omega^n}{n!}=e_1\wedge f_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_n\wedge f_n ,$$

which evaluates to $1$ on each positively oriented $g$-orthonormal frame.

**Complex dimension zero.** For $n=0$ a complex manifold is a discrete space and
compactness makes it a finite set of points with its unique complex structure;
there are no tangent vectors and no forms of positive degree, $\omega=0$, and the
operators $L,\Lambda,\partial,\bar\partial,d,\partial^*,\bar\partial^*,d^*$ and
all Laplacians introduced below are zero. The Hodge star is the identity on
degree zero, and $dV$ is the counting measure.

**(2) Complex-valued forms and Kähler operators.** Let $X$ be compact Kähler.
Write $\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)$ for the complex-valued smooth $k$-forms, the
complex-linear extension of the real forms of
[[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]; the Hodge star $*$ of
[[def-riemannian-hodge-star]] extends complex-linearly, and for
$\alpha,\beta\in\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)$ the **integral inner product**

$$\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle=\int_X\alpha\wedge*\bar\beta$$

is complex-linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second; the
integral is that of
[[def-integral-of-a-compactly-supported-top-form-on-an-oriented-manifold]] and
the integrand is $\lvert\alpha\rvert^2\,dV$ when $\beta=\alpha$, so the pairing
is a positive definite Hermitian form. In holomorphic charts

$$\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}\Omega^{p,q}(X),\qquad d=\partial+\bar\partial ,$$

with $\partial$ and $\bar\partial$ of bidegree $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$
([[def-bigraded-complex-differential-forms]]); the decomposition is independent
of the holomorphic chart because holomorphic chart changes preserve bidegree.

Put $L=\omega\wedge$, so that $L:\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)\to\Omega^{k+2}(X;\mathbb C)$,
and let $\Lambda,\partial^*,\bar\partial^*,d^*$ be the formal adjoints of
$L,\partial,\bar\partial,d$ with respect to $\langle\,,\rangle$; existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[lem-formal-adjoints-of-differential-operators-exist-and-are-unique]], applied
to the bundle of complex-valued forms with the metric of
[[prop-riemannian-metrics-induce-metrics-on-dual-tensor-and-exterior-bundles]]
and the density $dV$. The **Laplacians** are

$$\Delta_d=dd^*+d^*d,\qquad \Delta_\partial=\partial\partial^*+\partial^*\partial,\qquad \Delta_{\bar\partial}=\bar\partial\bar\partial^*+\bar\partial^*\bar\partial ,$$

and $\epsilon(k)=(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}$.

**(3) Rational pure Hodge structures.** Let $k\in\mathbb Z$. A **rational pure
Hodge structure of weight $k$** is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-vector space
$V$ together with a direct-sum decomposition by $\mathbb C$-subspaces

$$V_{\mathbb C}=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}V^{p,q},\qquad \overline{V^{p,q}}=V^{q,p},$$

where conjugation is the $\mathbb C$-antilinear involution
$v\otimes\lambda\mapsto v\otimes\bar\lambda$. The sum is finite because
$V_{\mathbb C}$ is finite dimensional, and it is direct by definition. The **Weil
operator** $C$ is the $\mathbb C$-linear endomorphism of $V_{\mathbb C}$ acting
as $i^{p-q}$ on $V^{p,q}$; the conjugation symmetry makes $C$ commute with
conjugation, so $C$ is the complexification of a real-linear endomorphism
of $V_{\mathbb R}=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$. It need not preserve $V$.

A **polarization** of such a Hodge structure is a nondegenerate $\mathbb Q$-bilinear
form $Q:V\times V\to\mathbb Q$, extended $\mathbb C$-bilinearly to $V_{\mathbb C}$,
such that

- $Q(y,x)=(-1)^kQ(x,y)$ for all $x,y$;
- $Q(V^{p,q},V^{a,b})=0$ unless $(a,b)=(q,p)$;
- $h(x,y)=Q(Cx,\bar y)$ is a positive definite Hermitian form on $V_{\mathbb C}$.

A **rational sub-Hodge structure** is a $\mathbb Q$-subspace
$U\subseteq V$ with $U_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}(U_{\mathbb C}\cap V^{p,q})$.
The **Tate shift** $V(-r)$, for $r\in\mathbb Z$, keeps the underlying $\mathbb Q$-vector
space, the Weil operator and $Q$ as they are and moves the bidegrees to
$(p+r,q+r)$, so that the weight becomes $k+2r$; equivalently, $(V(-r))^{p,q}=V^{p-r,q-r}$.

With the conventions of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]], all
structures in this item are rational pure Hodge structures
$(V,\{V^{p,q}\})$, $V_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}V^{p,q}$, of one fixed
weight $k$; write $f_{\mathbb C}$ for the $\mathbb C$-linear extension of a
$\mathbb Q$-linear map.

A **morphism of Hodge structures** $f:(V,\{V^{p,q}\})\to(W,\{W^{p,q}\})$ is a
$\mathbb Q$-linear map $f:V\to W$ whose $\mathbb C$-linear extension satisfies
$$f_{\mathbb C}(V^{p,q})\subseteq W^{p,q}\qquad(p+q=k).$$
**Kernels and images** of such a morphism are again rational sub-Hodge
structures: writing $x=\sum_{p+q=k}x^{p,q}$ with $x^{p,q}\in V^{p,q}$, the
relation $0=f_{\mathbb C}(x)=\sum_{p+q=k}f_{\mathbb C}(x^{p,q})$ with
$f_{\mathbb C}(x^{p,q})\in W^{p,q}$ forces $f_{\mathbb C}(x^{p,q})=0$ for every
$(p,q)$, because the sum decomposition of $W_{\mathbb C}$ is direct, so
$$\ker(f_{\mathbb C})=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}\bigl(\ker(f_{\mathbb C})\cap V^{p,q}\bigr);$$
and $\operatorname{im}(f_{\mathbb C})=\sum_{p+q=k}f_{\mathbb C}(V^{p,q})$ is
direct, since $f_{\mathbb C}(V^{p,q})\subseteq W^{p,q}$ and the target
bidegrees of a direct sum are distinct, so
$$\operatorname{im}(f_{\mathbb C})=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}\bigl(\operatorname{im}(f_{\mathbb C})\cap W^{p,q}\bigr).$$
The **direct sum** $V\oplus W$ is the Hodge structure of the same weight $k$
with $(V\oplus W)^{p,q}=V^{p,q}\oplus W^{p,q}$, the inclusions and projections
being morphisms.

A **short exact sequence** $0\to U\xrightarrow{\,i\,}V\xrightarrow{\,\pi\,}W\to0$
of Hodge structures of weight $k$ consists of morphisms that are exact as a
sequence of $\mathbb Q$-vector spaces. It **splits** in the category of Hodge
structures if $\pi$ admits a morphism $s:W\to V$ with
$\pi\circ s=\operatorname{id}_W$. A Hodge structure is **polarizable** if it
admits a polarization, and **simple** if it has no nonzero proper rational
sub-Hodge structure, that is, no $\mathbb Q$-subspace $U\subseteq V$ with
$U\ne0,V$ and
$U_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}(U_{\mathbb C}\cap V^{p,q})$.

derivations.claim: The Weil operator $C$ preserves $U_{\mathbb C}$, because $U_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}(U_{\mathbb C}\cap V^{p,q})$ and $C$ multiplies each $U_{\mathbb C}\cap V^{p,q}$ by the scalar $i^{p-q}$; complex conjugation preserves $U_{\mathbb C}$ because it exchanges $V^{p,q}$ with $V^{q,p}$ and preserves $U_{\mathbb C}$

Since $Q|_U$ is nondegenerate by step 1.1, the rational equations $Q(x,U)=0$ define a rational subspace $U^{\perp_Q}$ whose dimension is $\dim V-\dim U$, the kernel of the surjective pairing map $V\to U^{\vee}$, $x\mapsto Q(x,\cdot)|_U$, having that dimension; and $U\cap U^{\perp_Q}=0$ because $Q|_U$ is nondegenerate. Hence $V=U\oplus U^{\perp_Q}$ as $\mathbb Q$-vector spaces. Let $x=\sum_{p+q=k}x^{p,q}\in U^{\perp_Q}_{\mathbb C}$ with $x^{p,q}\in V^{p,q}$, and fix $(r,s)$; for every $v\in U^{s,r}$ one has $$0=Q(x,v)=\sum_{p+q=k}Q(x^{p,q},v)=Q(x^{r,s},v),$$ because $Q$ pairs $V^{p,q}$ only with $V^{q,p}$
Let $0\to U\xrightarrow{i}V\xrightarrow{\pi}W\to0$ be a short exact sequence of polarizable rational pure Hodge structures of the fixed weight $k$

For semisimplicity, suppose $V\ne0$ is polarizable. Among the nonzero rational sub-Hodge structures of $V$ the dimensions form a nonempty subset of $\{1,\dots,\dim V\}$, so there is one, $U$, of least dimension; then $U$ is simple, since a nonzero rational sub-Hodge structure of $U$ is one of $V$ of no larger dimension. Positivity is used only over $\mathbb R$ and is not invoked over $F$, and no new subobject of $V_F$ is claimed to descend to $V$. The argument is finite-dimensional rational and complex linear algebra on fixed finite-dimensional structures and uses no choice principle.

Step 2.1 treats $x=0$, and the radical of step 1.1 is exactly the kernel of the nondegenerate form $Q|_U$, so only $u=0$ lies in it.
A one-dimensional polarizable $V$ is simple in step 4.1, since a nonzero rational sub-Hodge structure has the same dimension.
Degenerate forms cannot occur: step 1.1 proves the radical of $Q|_U$ is zero and step 2.1 proves $U\cap U^{\perp_Q}=0$.
The statement has no ordered or degree endpoints; the weight $k$ is fixed and the semisimplicity induction of step 4.1 terminates at the endpoints $U^{\perp_Q}=0$ and $\dim V=1$.

is positive, and the local orientations therefore glue along holomorphic charts
to a global orientation of $X$. Let $v_1,\dots,v_n$ be a $g$-orthonormal complex
frame, so $g(v_j,v_k)=\delta_{jk}$ and $g(v_j,Jv_k)=0$, and let $e_j=g(v_j,\cdot)$ and
$f_j=g(Jv_j,\cdot)$ be the metric-dual covectors. Then
$(e_1,f_1,\dots,e_n,f_n)$ is a positively oriented $g$-orthonormal coframe,
$f_j=-Je_j$ for the pullback action $(J\alpha)(v)=\alpha(Jv)$ of $J$ on
covectors, and

$$\omega=\sum_{j=1}^n e_j\wedge f_j .$$

The **oriented volume form** is the top form

$$dV:=\frac{\omega^n}{n!}=e_1\wedge f_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_n\wedge f_n ,$$

which evaluates to $1$ on each positively oriented $g$-orthonormal frame.

**Complex dimension zero.** For $n=0$ a complex manifold is a discrete space and
compactness makes it a finite set of points with its unique complex structure;
there are no tangent vectors and no forms of positive degree, $\omega=0$, and the
operators $L,\Lambda,\partial,\bar\partial,d,\partial^*,\bar\partial^*,d^*$ and
all Laplacians introduced below are zero. The Hodge star is the identity on
degree zero, and $dV$ is the counting measure.

**(2) Complex-valued forms and Kähler operators.** Let $X$ be compact Kähler.
Write $\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)$ for the complex-valued smooth $k$-forms, the
complex-linear extension of the real forms of
[[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]; the Hodge star $*$ of
[[def-riemannian-hodge-star]] extends complex-linearly, and for
$\alpha,\beta\in\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)$ the **integral inner product**

$$\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle=\int_X\alpha\wedge*\bar\beta$$

is complex-linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second; the
integral is that of
[[def-integral-of-a-compactly-supported-top-form-on-an-oriented-manifold]] and
the integrand is $\lvert\alpha\rvert^2\,dV$ when $\beta=\alpha$, so the pairing
is a positive definite Hermitian form. In holomorphic charts

$$\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}\Omega^{p,q}(X),\qquad d=\partial+\bar\partial ,$$

with $\partial$ and $\bar\partial$ of bidegree $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$
([[def-bigraded-complex-differential-forms]]); the decomposition is independent
of the holomorphic chart because holomorphic chart changes preserve bidegree.

Put $L=\omega\wedge$, so that $L:\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)\to\Omega^{k+2}(X;\mathbb C)$,
and let $\Lambda,\partial^*,\bar\partial^*,d^*$ be the formal adjoints of
$L,\partial,\bar\partial,d$ with respect to $\langle\,,\rangle$; existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[lem-formal-adjoints-of-differential-operators-exist-and-are-unique]], applied
to the bundle of complex-valued forms with the metric of
[[prop-riemannian-metrics-induce-metrics-on-dual-tensor-and-exterior-bundles]]
and the density $dV$. The **Laplacians** are

$$\Delta_d=dd^*+d^*d,\qquad \Delta_\partial=\partial\partial^*+\partial^*\partial,\qquad \Delta_{\bar\partial}=\bar\partial\bar\partial^*+\bar\partial^*\bar\partial ,$$

and $\epsilon(k)=(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}$.

**(3) Rational pure Hodge structures.** Let $k\in\mathbb Z$. A **rational pure
Hodge structure of weight $k$** is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-vector space
$V$ together with a direct-sum decomposition by $\mathbb C$-subspaces

$$V_{\mathbb C}=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}V^{p,q},\qquad \overline{V^{p,q}}=V^{q,p},$$

where conjugation is the $\mathbb C$-antilinear involution
$v\otimes\lambda\mapsto v\otimes\bar\lambda$. The sum is finite because
$V_{\mathbb C}$ is finite dimensional, and it is direct by definition. The **Weil
operator** $C$ is the $\mathbb C$-linear endomorphism of $V_{\mathbb C}$ acting
as $i^{p-q}$ on $V^{p,q}$; the conjugation symmetry makes $C$ commute with
conjugation, so $C$ is the complexification of a real-linear endomorphism
of $V_{\mathbb R}=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$. It need not preserve $V$.

A **polarization** of such a Hodge structure is a nondegenerate $\mathbb Q$-bilinear
form $Q:V\times V\to\mathbb Q$, extended $\mathbb C$-bilinearly to $V_{\mathbb C}$,
such that

- $Q(y,x)=(-1)^kQ(x,y)$ for all $x,y$;
- $Q(V^{p,q},V^{a,b})=0$ unless $(a,b)=(q,p)$;
- $h(x,y)=Q(Cx,\bar y)$ is a positive definite Hermitian form on $V_{\mathbb C}$.

A **rational sub-Hodge structure** is a $\mathbb Q$-subspace
$U\subseteq V$ with $U_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}(U_{\mathbb C}\cap V^{p,q})$.
The **Tate shift** $V(-r)$, for $r\in\mathbb Z$, keeps the underlying $\mathbb Q$-vector
space, the Weil operator and $Q$ as they are and moves the bidegrees to
$(p+r,q+r)$, so that the weight becomes $k+2r$; equivalently, $(V(-r))^{p,q}=V^{p-r,q-r}$.

Let $m\ge1$. A **chart** on a topological space $X$ is a homeomorphism
$\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ from an open set $U\subseteq X$ onto an open subset of
$\mathbb C^m$ with its usual topology ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]);
two charts $\varphi,\psi$ are **holomorphically compatible** when the
transition maps $\psi\circ\varphi^{-1}$ and $\varphi\circ\psi^{-1}$ are
holomorphic on the open sets where they are defined
([[def-holomorphic-function-in-several-complex-variables]]). A **holomorphic
atlas** is a family of pairwise compatible charts whose domains cover $X$. A
**complex manifold of dimension $m$** is a nonempty Hausdorff
([[def-hausdorff-space]]) second-countable ([[def-second-countable-space]])
topological space carrying a holomorphic atlas; the same maximal-atlas argument
as for [[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]] applies verbatim with
$\mathbb C^m$ in place of $\mathbb C$: the union of a holomorphic atlas with all
charts compatible with it is again a holomorphic atlas, so one passes to the
unique maximal atlas and calls its members holomorphic charts. Each chart is a
homeomorphism onto an open subset of $\mathbb C^m\cong\mathbb R^{2m}$, so $X$ is
a topological manifold without boundary of real dimension $2m$
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]), and for connected $X$ the case
$m=1$ recovers Riemann surfaces ([[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]]).

A **holomorphic map** $f:X\to Y$ between complex manifolds is a continuous map
whose expression in every pair of holomorphic charts is holomorphic
([[def-holomorphic-map-and-complex-jacobian]]); equivalently, for every open
$V\subseteq Y$ and every holomorphic function $h$ on $V$, the function
$h\circ f$ is holomorphic on $f^{-1}(V)$. The forward implication is the
holomorphic chain rule; conversely apply this condition to the coordinate
functions of a chart on $Y$.

**Induced smooth structure and complex structure.** Holomorphic functions on
open subsets of $\mathbb C^m$ are smooth
([[cor-holomorphic-functions-in-several-variables-are-smooth]]), so every
holomorphic atlas is a smooth atlas ([[def-smooth-atlas]]) and $X$ is a smooth
manifold of real dimension $2m$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]) whose smooth charts
include the holomorphic ones. In holomorphic coordinates
$z_k=x_k+iy_k$ the **complex structure** is the endomorphism field $J$ of the
tangent bundle determined by $J\partial_{x_k}=\partial_{y_k}$ and
$J\partial_{y_k}=-\partial_{x_k}$; it satisfies $J^2=-\mathrm{id}$ and is
independent of the holomorphic chart, because a holomorphic transition map has
complex-linear differential ([[def-holomorphic-map-and-complex-jacobian]],
[[thm-chain-rule-for-holomorphic-maps-in-several-variables]]) and complex-linear
maps intertwine the two coordinate definitions of multiplication by $i$. A
**Hermitian metric** on $X$ is a Riemannian metric $g$
([[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]) satisfying
$g(Jv,Jw)=g(v,w)$ for all tangent vectors $v,w$; its Riemannian volume density
is written $\mu_g$ ([[def-riemannian-volume-density]]). The complex structure
makes each tangent space a complex vector space, so the tangent bundle is a
smooth complex vector bundle in the sense of
[[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]].

**Holomorphic vector bundles and Hermitian bundle metrics.** A **holomorphic
vector bundle of rank $r$** on $X$ is a smooth complex vector bundle
$\pi:E\to X$ of rank $r$
([[def-smooth-vector-bundle-rank-fibre-and-trivial-bundle]],
[[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]]) together with an open
cover $(V_\alpha)$ of $X$ and smooth local trivializations
$\theta_\alpha:E|_{V_\alpha}\to V_\alpha\times\mathbb C^r$ whose transition
matrices $g_{\alpha\beta}:V_\alpha\cap V_\beta\to\mathrm{GL}_r(\mathbb C)$,
defined by $\theta_\alpha\theta_\beta^{-1}(p,v)=(p,g_{\alpha\beta}(p)v)$, are
holomorphic. A **holomorphic frame** over an open set $V$ is a smooth
complex-linear trivialization whose transition matrices with the supplied
trivializations are holomorphic on every overlap. Changing holomorphic frame multiplies a local section by a
holomorphic matrix, hence a smooth local section is **holomorphic** exactly when
its representatives in holomorphic frames are holomorphic functions. A
**Hermitian metric** $h$ on $E$ is a smooth bundle metric
([[def-smooth-bundle-metric]]) whose fibre pairings are positive definite
Hermitian forms, linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the
second; the condition is frame-independent because the gauge freedom is
conjugation by a pointwise invertible matrix. Smooth sections are
$\Gamma(E)$ ([[def-smooth-section-local-section-and-support]]).

For an integer $n\ge1$, **complex projective space** is the set of complex lines in $\mathbb C^{n+1}$ with the quotient topology
$$\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C):=(\mathbb C^{n+1}\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb C^\times,\qquad [z_0:\cdots:z_n]:=\mathbb C^\times(z_0,\ldots,z_n).$$
The quotient projection is continuous and surjective. Its restriction to the unit sphere $S^{2n+1}\subset\mathbb C^{n+1}$ is still surjective, so $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ is compact. It is Hausdorff: the map sending a nonzero vector $z$ to the orthogonal projection $zz^*/\lVert z\rVert^2$ is continuous and constant on each complex line, hence descends by the quotient topology to a continuous injection from $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ into the Hausdorff space of complex matrices. A continuous injection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism onto its image.

For open $V\subseteq\mathbb C^r$, a map $H:V\to\mathbb C^s$ is **holomorphic** if at every $a\in V$ there is a complex-linear map $A_a:\mathbb C^r\to\mathbb C^s$ such that $H(a+h)=H(a)+A_a h+R_a(h)$ with $\lVert R_a(h)\rVert/\lVert h\rVert\to0$ as $h\to0$, $h\ne0$. When $r=1$, this is equivalent to each component being holomorphic in the sense of [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]], since a finite vector of scalar difference quotients converges exactly when each component does. A complex atlas consists of charts into $\mathbb C^n$ with holomorphic transitions in both directions.

For $j\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$ let $U_j:=\{[z_0:\cdots:z_n]:z_j\ne0\}$. These open sets cover projective space: their inverse images under the quotient projection are the open saturated sets where $z_j\ne0$. The **standard chart** is
$$\varphi_j:U_j\longrightarrow\mathbb C^n,\qquad [z_0:\cdots:z_n]\longmapsto (z_0/z_j,\ldots,\widehat{z_j/z_j},\ldots,z_n/z_j),$$
where the $j$th coordinate is omitted. It is well defined under rescaling. The coordinate-ratio map on the inverse image of $U_j$ is continuous and constant on each quotient fibre, so the quotient topology makes $\varphi_j$ continuous; its inverse inserts $1$ in the $j$th position and is continuous by composition with the quotient projection. Hence it is a homeomorphism. On $U_j\cap U_k$ the transition from the $j$th chart to the $k$th chart sends each coordinate $w_\ell=z_\ell/z_j$ ($\ell\ne j$) to $w_\ell/w_k$ for $\ell\ne k$, with the omitted $j$th coordinate equal to $1/w_k$. To check holomorphy at $a$ with $a_k\ne0$, set $a_j=1$ and $h_j=0$ for the omitted source coordinate. Each target coordinate has the expansion $(a_\ell+h_\ell)/(a_k+h_k)=a_\ell/a_k+h_\ell/a_k-a_\ell h_k/a_k^2+O(\lVert h\rVert^2)$ for $\ell\ne k$. The linear term is complex-linear, and the remainder estimate follows by expanding the reciprocal at the nonzero $a_k$. The inverse transition has the same form, so both are holomorphic. Thus these charts make $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ a complex manifold of complex dimension $n$ and a topological manifold of real dimension $2n$ in the sense of [[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]. The finite chart cover by second-countable copies of $\mathbb C^n$ gives a countable base. Its rational transition functions have smooth real coordinate expressions on their domains, so the atlas also defines the smooth structure in the sense of [[def-smooth-manifold]]. The space is path-connected: distinct lines represented by $u,v$ give the path $t\mapsto[(1-t)u+tv]$, whose vector never vanishes because $u,v$ are linearly independent; equal lines give a constant path. In particular, $\mathbb P^1(\mathbb C)$ is a Riemann surface in the sense of [[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]].

A map $F:X\to\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ from a Riemann surface is **holomorphic** when it is continuous and every component of each chart expression $\varphi_j\circ F$, written in a local coordinate of $X$, is holomorphic on the open set $F^{-1}(U_j)$. On an overlap, the new components are $f_\ell/f_k$ and $1/f_k$, where the $f_\ell$ are the old components and $f_k\ne0$. The scalar quotient rule gives their holomorphy ([[thm-algebra-of-complex-derivatives]]), so it suffices to check one target chart locally. Changing the source coordinate composes each scalar component with a one-variable holomorphic chart transition, where [[thm-chain-rule-for-complex-derivatives]] applies ([[def-holomorphic-and-meromorphic-map-of-riemann-surfaces]]). A **projective line** is the image in $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ of a two-dimensional complex subspace of $\mathbb C^{n+1}$. Every invertible linear map of $\mathbb C^{n+1}$ induces a holomorphic projective linear transformation: in source and target standard charts its coordinates are ratios of affine-linear functions with nonzero denominator, and the same reciprocal expansion gives a complex-linear derivative; these transformations act transitively on $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism locally of
finite presentation ([[def-locally-finite-presentation-morphism]]) and let
$x\in X$ with $s=f(x)$. Then $f$ is smooth at $x$
([[def-smooth-morphism-schemes]]) if and only if there are affine open
neighbourhoods $U=\operatorname{Spec}C$ of $x$ and
$V=\operatorname{Spec}A$ of $s$ with $f(U)\subseteq V$ and a presentation of
$C_h$, for some $h\in C\smallsetminus\mathfrak q$ with $\mathfrak q$ the prime
of $x$, as
$$C_h\;\cong\;\Bigl(A[t_1,\dots,t_m]/(f_1,\dots,f_r)\Bigr)_g,$$
in which some $r\times r$ minor of the Jacobian matrix
$\bigl(\partial f_j/\partial t_i\bigr)$ has image a unit of $C_h$. Such a chart
is flat over $A$ with geometrically regular fibres whose components have
dimension $m-r$; in the local-dimension convention of
[[def-relative-dimension-smooth-morphism]] it exhibits relative dimension
$m-r$ at $x$.

The criterion demands that *some* presentation have an invertible $r\times r$
minor; it does not demand this of an arbitrary redundant equation list, and
$r>m$ makes an invertible $r\times r$ minor impossible by definition of the
matrix shape.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m\times\mathbb C^n$ be open, let
$f:U\to\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic, and let $(a,b)\in U$ satisfy $f(a,b)=0$.
Assume the complex Jacobian with respect to the second block is invertible:

$$\det\left(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial w_k}(a,b)\right)_{1\le j,k\le n}\ne0.$$

Then there are neighbourhoods $A$ of $a$ and $B$ of $b$, and a unique
holomorphic map $\varphi:A\to B$, such that

$$f(z,\varphi(z))=0\qquad(z\in A),$$

and, after shrinking $A\times B$ if needed,

$$f(z,w)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=\varphi(z).$$

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb C^m$ be
holomorphic, and let $a\in U$. If $\det J_{\mathbb C}F(a)\ne0$, then there are
open neighbourhoods $U_0\subseteq U$ of $a$ and $V_0$ of $F(a)$ such that
$F|_{U_0}:U_0\to V_0$ is biholomorphic.

If $G:V_0\to U_0$ denotes the inverse, then

$$DG(w)=DF(G(w))^{-1}\qquad(w\in V_0).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice as inherited from the projective-space and sheaf
constructions ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $S$ be a Noetherian scheme
([[def-locally-noetherian-and-noetherian-scheme]]), let $f:X\to S$ be a proper
morphism of finite type ([[def-proper-morphism]]) and let $L$ be an invertible
$\mathcal O_X$-module ([[def-invertible-sheaf]]) that is ample on $X$
([[def-ample-invertible-sheaf]]). Write
$$A=\Gamma_*(X,L)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\Gamma(X,L^{\otimes n}),\qquad A_+=\bigoplus_{n\ge1}\Gamma(X,L^{\otimes n}),$$
and for $a\in\Gamma(X,L^{\otimes n})$ with $n\ge1$ let
$X_a=\{\,x\in X:\text{the image of }a\text{ in }L^{\otimes n}\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}\kappa(x)\text{ is nonzero}\,\}$
be its nonvanishing locus.

Then there is an integer $d_0\ge1$ such that for every $d\ge d_0$ the sheaf
$L^{\otimes d}$ is **closed H-very ample relative to $S$**
([[def-very-ample-invertible-sheaf-relative]]): there are an integer $N_d\ge0$
and a finite family of global sections of $L^{\otimes d}$ whose associated
$S$-morphism $X\to\mathbb P^{N_d}_S$ is a closed immersion with
$\mathcal O(1)$ pulling back to $L^{\otimes d}$.

The ampleness used is ampleness of $L$ on $X$ itself; $f$-ampleness over a
non-affine base is not substituted. Every scheme in sight may be empty: if
$X=\varnothing$, then $L$ is ample vacuously and the empty morphism shows that
every $L^{\otimes d}$ is closed H-very ample relative to $S$, so that in this
case $d_0=1$ works.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional Hausdorff
second-countable smooth manifold, possibly with boundary or empty, and let
$L\to M$ be a smooth complex line bundle with a supplied Hermitian metric and
Hermitian connection $\nabla$. Write $\Omega_\nabla$ for its curvature and
$c_1(L):=e(L_{\mathbb R})$ for the published integral line class, using the
complex orientation on the underlying real plane. Let
$$\rho_M:H^2(M;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow H^2(M;\mathbb R)$$
be induced by $\mathbb Z\hookrightarrow\mathbb R$. Under the natural de Rham
isomorphism $J_M$,
$$J_M\left[ -\frac{\Omega_\nabla}{2\pi i}\right]=\rho_M(c_1(L)).$$
For a disconnected base the same line-class convention is understood on each
component; the global class is the Euler class displayed above.

If $\nabla'$ is any complex connection on $L$, not necessarily metric
compatible, then
$$\left[-\frac{\Omega_{\nabla'}}{2\pi i}\right]=\iota_M\!\left(J_M^{-1}\rho_M(c_1(L))\right)\quad\text{in }H^2_{\rm dR}(M;\mathbb C),$$
where $\iota_M$ is induced by including real-valued forms into complex-valued
forms. Thus the arbitrary-connection class is identified with the same real
class by the degree-one transgression.

Let $E\to M$ be a smooth real vector bundle of rank $2r$, where $r\geq0$,
over a smooth manifold that may have boundary. A **smooth complex structure**
on $E$ is a smooth bundle endomorphism $J:E\to E$ with $J^2=-I$. It makes
each fiber a complex vector space by $(a+ib)v=av+bJv$. Equivalently, $E$ has
local smooth complex frames with transition maps in $\operatorname{GL}_r(\mathbb C)$. In one direction, multiplication by $i$ in complex bundle charts gives
such a smooth $J$ because the transition maps are complex-linear. Conversely,
near any point choose a complex basis in its fiber and extend its vectors to
local smooth real sections; those sections together with their $J$-images
remain a real frame after shrinking the neighborhood, and give a local complex
frame. Forgetting smoothness in these charts gives the associated rank-$r$
complex topological vector bundle of
[[def-real-and-complex-topological-vector-bundle]].

For a smooth complex bundle $(E,J)$, write $\Gamma_{\mathbb C}(E)$ for its
smooth complex sections. A **complex connection** is a covariant derivative
$\nabla:\Gamma_{\mathbb C}(E)\to\Omega^1(M;E)$ that is $\mathbb C$-linear
and satisfies
$$\nabla(fs)=df\otimes s+f\nabla s$$
for every smooth complex-valued function $f$ and section $s$. This extends the
real bundle-connection convention of
[[def-connection-on-a-smooth-vector-bundle]]. A complex connection is
**Hermitian** for a supplied Hermitian metric $h$, taken linear in its first
variable and conjugate-linear in its second, when
$$Xh(s,t)=h(\nabla_Xs,t)+h(s,\nabla_Xt)$$
for all smooth sections $s,t$ and vector fields $X$. A real connection on a
Euclidean vector bundle is **Euclidean-compatible** when it obeys the same
identity for the real bundle metric, as in
[[def-metric-compatible-connection-on-a-riemannian-vector-bundle]].

Let $E\to M$ be a smooth vector bundle with connection $\nabla$. For smooth
vector fields $X,Y$ and a smooth section $s$ of $E$, the **curvature of
$\nabla$** is

$$R^\nabla(X,Y)s:=\nabla_X\nabla_Ys-\nabla_Y\nabla_Xs-\nabla_{[X,Y]}s.$$

This uses the same sign convention as the curvature of an affine connection.
The next proposition proves that this operator is tensorial and hence is an
$\operatorname{End}(E)$-valued two-form. At this definition stage no metric,
torsion, or bundle trivialization is assumed.

If $M$ is empty, $E$ has rank zero, or $M$ has dimension zero, the displayed
operator is the unique zero curvature operator. For a rank-one bundle and for
a manifold with boundary the same local formula applies without modification.

Assume AC. Let $L,M$ be numerable complex line bundles over a path-connected
CW complex with a vertex basepoint, or over a path-connected paracompact
Hausdorff CGWH space of CW homotopy type. Then
$$c_1(L\otimes M)=c_1(L)+c_1(M),\qquad c_1(L^*)=-c_1(L),\qquad c_1(\overline L)=-c_1(L),$$
where $L^*$ is the dual line and $\overline L$ the conjugate line.

Assume AC. For a compact smooth manifold $X$, the natural coefficient maps
induce isomorphisms $H^k(X;\mathbb Q)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}F\cong H^k(X;F)$ for
every characteristic-zero field $F$, finite-dimensional in each degree. For
$F=\mathbb R,\mathbb C$ these identify singular cohomology with the real or
complex de Rham cohomology. They preserve cup products and are natural for maps
between such manifolds. No ordered-field or positivity structure is asserted
for a general $F$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

In a nonzero commutative ring, every proper ideal is contained in a maximal ideal.

Let $k$ be a field, let $A$ be a finite-type $k$-algebra, and let
$\mathfrak m$ be a maximal ideal of $A$. Then the residue field $A/\mathfrak m$
is a finite extension of $k$.

Every nonconstant complex polynomial has a complex root.

This proof uses Liouville's theorem and is independent of the minimum-modulus proof cited in the accompanying agreement remark.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC). Let $i:Z\to Y$ be a closed immersion, where
closed immersion has the published convention that the map on structure sheaves
is surjective. For every affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ of $Y$, there is
a unique ideal $I\subseteq A$ such that, over $U$,
$$i^{-1}(U)\cong\operatorname{Spec}(A/I).$$
Conversely, every quotient map $A\to A/I$ induces a closed immersion
$\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)\to\operatorname{Spec}A$. Every base change of a
closed immersion is a closed immersion. In particular, the empty subscheme of
$\operatorname{Spec}A$ corresponds to $I=A$.

Let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism of schemes and let
$\Delta_{X/S}:X\to X\times_S X$ be its diagonal morphism
([[def-diagonal-morphism-scheme]]).

- $f$ is **separated** if $\Delta_{X/S}$ is a closed immersion
  ([[def-closed-immersion-schemes]]).
- $f$ is **quasi-separated** if $\Delta_{X/S}$ is a quasi-compact morphism
  ([[def-quasi-compact-and-quasi-separated-morphism]]).

A scheme $Y$ is called separated, respectively quasi-separated, when the
structure morphism $Y\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z$ is separated, respectively
quasi-separated. The affine-intersection condition recorded under
[[def-quasi-compact-and-quasi-separated-morphism]] is the earlier definition;
its equivalence to quasi-compactness of $\Delta_{X/S}$ is proved in
[[lem-diagonal-quasi-compact-iff-quasi-separated]] on this page. Both properties are
properties of the morphism $f$ and of its diagonal, and neither is a condition
on the point-set topology of $X$ alone.

Assume AC. Every finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold, including a manifold with boundary and the empty manifold, is paracompact Hausdorff, compactly generated weak Hausdorff, and has the homotopy type of a CW complex. Every smooth finite-rank vector bundle on it is numerable.

derivations.claim: Let $x\in X(\mathbb C)$ be a closed point. Since $X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$ is smooth and locally of finite presentation, the Jacobian criterion

On the standard chart $U_j\cong\mathbb C^N$ of $\mathbb P^N(\mathbb C)$ put $\omega_{\mathrm{FS}}:=\frac{i}{2\pi}\partial\bar\partial\log(1+|z^{(j)}|^2)$, $|z^{(j)}|^2=\sum_l|z^{(j)}_l|^2$. On an overlap one has $1+|z^{(j)}|^2=|h|^2(1+|z^{(k)}|^2)$ for the nonvanishing holomorphic function $h=Z_k/Z_j$, and $\partial\bar\partial\log|h|^2=0$ because locally one can choose a holomorphic logarithm of $h$: near a point write $h=h_0(1+v)$ with $|v|<1$ and use the convergent power series for $\log(1+v)$; then $\log|h|^2$ is a constant plus that holomorphic logarithm and its conjugate; hence the local forms agree on overlaps and define a global smooth real form of type $(1,1)$ on $\mathbb P^N(\mathbb C)$

On overlaps, regular coordinate functions are locally fractions with nonvanishing denominators, hence holomorphic on the graph charts of step 1.1; the reverse transition is obtained in the same way. Zariski-open subsets are open for this topology, because on an affine presentation their complements are polynomial zero loci. This gives compatible local holomorphic atlases.
